entries.title: About the Course
entries.content:
This course includes the following topic(s): Canadian History: Grades 9-10, World History: Grades 10-12, Ancient History: Grades 10-12

About Canadian History: Grades 9-10
Read about Canadian history from 1800-1900 through books that immerse students in the time period and allow them to see the world through the eyes of those who lived it. Through engaging narratives, biographies, history spines, primary source documents, oral histories, historical fiction, and books that show different perspectives, students come to see history as more than dates and events and develop relationships with people from the past. Viewing images, looking at maps, and working on one's Book of Centuries are also part of developing this relationship.

About World History: Grades 10-12
Read about world history from 1800-1900. View images and reference atlases and maps to set the people and events in their time and place. Update History Charts and Book of Centuries.

About Ancient History: Grades 10-12
Drawing on material culture, primary sources, and wider overviews, this course delves into the time period from 100 BC to 350 AD.

• Take a second to recall what you read previously in the same book or topic.

• If the previous passage is difficult to remember, try looking back at any chapter/section headings or illustrations or reading the first paragraph to jog the memory.

• Read the selection assigned OR read for the number of minutes allocated, leaving time for narration and mapwork. Use whichever guide (i.e., pages or minutes) works best for you. You want to read enough to be interesting, but not so much that you feel overwhelmed.

• If a book is challenging for you as a student, try stopping to narrate to yourself silently for a minute every now and then to make sure you are tracking. You might also want to read aloud to yourself. Or you might want to listen to an audiobook version of the text and read along with it. 

• If a book is an easy read, enjoy the ride! 

• Keep an eye out for quotes to put in your commonplace book or events or characters to put down in your Book of Centuries.

• Process and integrate your reading by narrating either orally or in writing. Some lesson plans will give you a suggestion of how best to narrate. 

• To keep yourself on track, you might want to set a timer, so you stop reading with enough time to narrate.

• After your narration, think about how what you read connects to other subjects, other books, and other things you've read, watched, or seen in the past or present. 

• Share any ideas that are particularly interesting to you with your fellow classmates, teachers, parents, friends, or others. You might even want to do a bit more reading or research on something on your own time in the afternoon or evenings.

These lessons are written directly to the student, but to assist them throughout the year, please read through this section and the lesson plans so you are familiar with the instructions and flow of the lessons. Accountability components are added to facilitate teacher/student discussion and growing independence. 

Those educating at home might pick one or two history lessons to read aloud with their students to keep up the habit of oral narration and foster conversation and relationship, and then simply give students these lesson plans and the rest of the books and check in with them throughout the term for conversation, support, and accountability. 

It is valuable for those in a classroom setting to also have a mix of lessons that students complete themselves silently and others read aloud and narrated together. Classroom settings lend themselves well to additional discussion and sharing at the end of lessons, after everyone has narrated either together or independently in writing.

lessons.title: 30m World History: Grades 10-12 - Lesson 1
lessons.body:
⍞ Materials: When America First Met China

➜ INTRO
One of the most important actions taken when creating a new nation is establishing trade with other countries. As a newly founded nation, that is exactly what the United States of America set out to do. The United States traded for things like silk, gold, and tea, while other nations traded for everything from sea otter and seal pelts to sandalwood, opium, cotton, and tortoiseshell. As the United States navigated new waters—both literally and figuratively—they would come into contact with a mighty trade nation that had a lot to offer them, including the ever-important tea that had become a household essential. However, China had its own rules and regulations as well as its own system of justice that was very different from the United States.
As you read through the chapter, we invite you to ponder what it must have been like to navigate these new waters and to meet new peoples whose way of life was so different from yours. What are the things you see in the text that surprise you? What things challenged your way of thinking? You will reflect on these questions after the reading.

➜ ANNOTATE
When America First Met China is a non-fiction book, which makes it a good candidate for annotation. While you are reading through the text, you may encounter an interesting point or main idea that you want to underline. You could put a question mark next to a statement you find unclear. You may place sticky notes on a page that you want to return to. Experiment with different ways to engage with the information in the book. Some students will record themselves reading or talking about the reading. Others may start a discussion with an acquaintance about the material. Try different ways and see what works and what doesn’t work for you. You can discuss your findings with your teacher.

➜ READ & NARRATE
Ch.6 p.146-160 "The return of peace" - “exotic name 'bêche-de-mer.'”

➜ MAP WORK
Familiarize yourself with the map at the beginning of When America First Met China. 

➜ WRITE
Answer the following questions in 3 paragraphs: What are the things you see in the text that surprise you? What things challenged your way of thinking? What things made you uncomfortable and why?

⍞ Materials: Underground Railroad

➜ INTRO
How do historians make discoveries about the past? The first book we will read this year - The Underground Railroad: Next Stop, Toronto! - explores what Toronto was like for African Americans seeking freedom in a new life in Canada. One aspect that makes this book so fascinating is that the authors show how they are able to learn about this period of history: there are lots of old photographs and newspaper articles from historical archives, but there was also an archaeological dig in downtown Toronto in 2015 that revealed a lot about who lived in Toronto during this period and how they lived. When we think of archaeology, we often think of discovering ruins from thousands of years ago, but archaeology also has a lot to teach us about our more recent past!

➜ READ, NARRATE, & DISCUSS
p.1-13 "The colored people" - "to live with them in Canada."

• How was Toronto involved in the larger story of the abolitionist movement?
• What did you learn about the life of Deborah Brown?

Sophie's Rebellion is a fictional account of one American girl's experience of the 1837-1838 Rebellions, as she is caught up in the Battle of Beauharnois. lessons.title: 40m Ancient History: Grades 10-12 - Lesson 2
lessons.body:
The Late Republic
⍞ Materials: Ancient Empires

➜ INTRO
Rome was founded in 753 BC, and it became a Republic in 509 BC. The Roman Republic had been involved in many wars. The most famous of these wars are known as the three Punic Wars. The Third Punic War was fought around 149-146 BC. During the Third Punic War, Rome would clash with a sovereign territory known as Carthage and ultimately would raze it to the ground. Rome would kill most of its male inhabitants and sell its women and children into slavery. With the defeat of Carthage, it would seem that Roman power was complete, as no other nation could stand in the way of its expansion.

However, the Roman Republic had internal issues. Its political and military leaders were corrupt, and despite its incredible growth, the Republic found itself in trouble. These political and military leaders were grasping for more power afforded them by their Republic governmental system. There were also internal struggles from people groups who refused to adapt to life under their new conquerors.

➜ ANNOTATE
Don't forget to annotate as you read.

➜ READ

lessons.title: 30m World History: Grades 10-12 - Lesson 6
lessons.body:
⍞ Materials: When America First Met China

➜ INTRO
A historian named Ian Barrow wrote a short history of the East India Company, which operated at the end of the sixteenth century all the way through the middle of the nineteenth. In his book, he writes about the beginning of this company, saying, "Toward the end of the sixteenth century, a group of English merchants based in London realized that there was an opportunity to make money in the spice trade." The British East India Company would exist for over 200 years and end up becoming one of the largest monopolies on trade. Additionally, it was known for having its own armies. The army at times reached 260,000 soldiers strong. 
The British government began to see the company for the threat it was and eliminated its monopoly in 1833. From then on, trade would look very different. The parliament would appoint people to government positions, and these men would be faced with many challenges as they sought to build ties with China amid a growing conflict.
*If you want to learn more or review the British East India Company, check out the short video provided in the Extra Helpings.

➜ ANNOTATE
Don't forget to annotate as you read.

➜ READ & NARRATE

lessons.body:
⍞ Materials: When America First Met China

➜ INTRO
One of the horrible parts about reading through history is coming face-to-face with the reality of sinful humanity. John Fea writes, "Indeed, anyone who studies the past realizes that there are no heroes in history. While people may perform heroic acts, all humans are tainted by sin and are susceptible to acting in ways that preference themselves over others and God. Historians understand, perhaps better than most, the reality of the pain, suffering, injustice, anger, and vice brought on by sin. In other words, they understand the tragic dimensions of life." 
Exploitation is just one of the many injustices taking place in the 1800s. As you read through the chapter, you are allowed to feel heartbroken, angry, and disappointed at the treatment of those who are also made in God's image. Both belief in Christ and in the depravity of humanity can help us better navigate history. As John Fea writes, "Similarly, a belief in depravity helps us to better explain the human condition—the restlessness, the search for meaning, and the prideful ambition that has defined much of the past, especially in the modern era. Augustine was quite correct when he opened his Confessions with the famous words, 'Our hearts are restless until they rest in you.'”

lessons.body:
⍞ Materials: Erebus

➜ INTRO
What happens when nations find themselves with war vessels, but no wars? For 1800s Britain, the answer was to send its ships on exploration missions. The Erebus was just one of the ships that made the transition from military vessel to a vessel used for research and exploration. The captains and crew of the vessel changed over the many years it spent on the seas.
In Erebus, you will read a book about a legendary ship. However, there is another benefit to Michael Palin’s book, which makes it a helpful read as well as an enjoyable one. Erebus does not just share the story of the ship itself, but of the world in which this ship sailed. As you read through Erebus, take note of the names being mentioned in each chapter.
I also invite you to adventure with the people on Erebus and on the HMS Terror. Pay attention to the letters and journals that are being mentioned and remember that these were real people who experienced a world very unlike our own. And yet, you’ll also see a world that is very familiar too.

➜ ANNOTATE
Erebus is a non-fiction book, which makes it a good candidate for annotation. While you are reading through the text, you may encounter an interesting point or main idea that you want to underline. You could put a question mark next to a statement you find unclear. You may place sticky notes on a page that you want to return to. Experiment with different ways to engage with the information in the book. Some students will record themselves reading or talking about the reading. Others may start a discussion with an acquaintance about the material. Try different ways and see what works and what doesn’t work for you. You can discuss your findings with your teacher.

➜ READ & NARRATE
Prologue-Ch.1 p.1-16

➜ WRITE
Write two paragraphs about the world figures and the events that you’ve read about in chapter one of Erebus. Who has appeared in the chapter? Why are they important? What is the historical setting of the book?

Introduction - Vanished Beyond the Map
⍞ Materials: Vanished Beyond the Map

➜ INTRO
Vanished Beyond the Map is an account of Adam Shoalts's quest to solve the mystery of what happened to Hubert Darrell, a long-forgotten explorer, trapper, guide, and mapmaker, who disappeared in the Arctic in 1910. Shoalts's narrative shows a historian at work: using archival research, historical documents, and interviews with elderly individuals who may have long-ago connections to Darrell's family, Shoalts pieces together Darrell's life and travels. But it is just as much a geographical story: Darrell immigrated from England to Manitoba, then journeyed to the Arctic following the Gold Rush. His life intersected with that of other great explorers, namely Roald Amundsen and Vilhjalmur Stefansson, and he travelled alone across vast distances in the Arctic.

Introduction to Early Church Writings and Clement
⍞ Materials: Early Christian Writings
 
➜ INTRO
Imagine uncovering the writing of an Early Church Father as you sift through a monastic library in the East, or as you begin to use that writing as a wrapping paper for raw fish and seafood. That is the reality of some of these texts translated in this collection of Early Christian Writers. 
These texts offer the modern-day reader more than early church doctrine and theology; they also offer us insights into the issues that the early church was facing as it began to follow the teachings of Christ. 

➜ NOTE
The first- and second-century Christians are operating in a world wholly different than our own. They are operating in empires that have different values, virtues, and myths. Moreover, these people are trying to figure out Jesus, his relationship to God, and the connection of the Holy Spirit; and they are operating with the Septuagint (The Greek Translation of the Hebrew Bible), the Gospels, and some of the letters. Keep in mind that the canon of the Bible will not be official until the late fourth century. 

As you read through these texts, take a moment to put your modern-day theological and biblical knowledge to the side. Listen to the words of these Christians. What are they asking? What are they teaching? Why might these be the questions that they are taking the time to answer? All of these questions can help us understand the early church world better and see where these early church writers are taking inspiration from.

The Didache
⍞ Materials: Early Christian Writings
 
➜ INTRO
Two very famous church fathers, known as Athanasius and Eusebius, have talked about the Didache as an apocryphal book, but that hasn't stopped its influence throughout the church's history. The Didache's influence in the early church cannot be understated. 

➜ NOTE
It is so easy to read these letters with our own time in mind. We invite you to set aside your modern-day mindset and try to read these letters with a 1st and 2nd-century mindset. terms.content:
Canadian History: Grades 9-10
· The Underground Railroad: Describe some of the ways historians have been able to learn about what life was like for freedom seekers who settled in Toronto. Include some specific details if possible. OR Tell all you know about one of the individuals or families you learned about from this book.

· Sophie's Rebellion: The novel features French Canadian, British, American, and English Canadian characters. Describe the attitudes and interactions of some of these groups towards each other, as depicted in the novel. OR Write a letter from Sophie to her father, describing all that happened in Beauharnois.

Ancient History: Grades 10-12
· Ancient Empires: In what ways does the Roman Republic remind you of your own country? In what ways is it different?

· Draw two pieces of art that you remember seeing this term. Briefly say what they are and describe them. What do you think they say about the cultures that they were a part of?

World History: Grades 10-12
· When America First Met China: Why was the invention of faster ships so important?

· When America First Met China: Describe the relationships between China and other countries in several paragraphs.

Canadian History: Grades 9-10
· The Charlottetown Conference: Describe how the Charlottetown Conference and the meetings that came after led to the founding of Canada in 1867. OR Choose one prominent figure you learned about who attended the Charlottetown Conference, and explain why their contribution to Canada's history was important.

· Vanished Beyond the Map: Imagine you are Hubert Darrell, packing for a journey, and can only take what you can pull on a sled. What do you pack? OR What does what you have learned about Darrell so far tell you about some of the challenges facing those who immigrated to the Canadian prairies in the late nineteenth century?

Ancient History: Grades 10-12
· Christians Reading Classics: Choose Cicero, Caesar, Tacitus, Perpetua, Suetonius, or Marcus Aurelius, and explore how their writings can influence the modern-day church today.

· Christians Reading Classics: How should Christians go about reading pagan classics? How can reading these classics benefit spiritual formation?

World History: Grades 10-12
· Erebus: Life on exploration was never easy. Yet, many people chose to pursue lives of exploration. What were the many reasons for people to pursue this lifestyle? Use examples from different characters to support your answer.

· Erebus: Choose one person from the narrative who fascinated you and summarize his or her story.

Canadian History: Grades 9-10
· Red Wolf: Write several paragraphs about how this story affected you. What will you take with you from reading it? Also, ponder the question: How does the messenger affect the sharing of the truths of the Gospel? Write a paragraph sharing your thoughts.

· Vanished Beyond the Map: Explain why explorers like Darrell, Hanbury, and Amundsen could successfully survive in the Arctic climate while others before them (like the Franklin Expedition) failed.

Ancient History: Grades 10-12
· Early Christian Writings: Based on the writings of the early church fathers that you have read this term, what were some of the primary concerns of the early church? What are the most common themes? Are the concerns of the early church the same as or different than the concerns of the Christian church today?

· Early Christian Writings: Summarize one letter of your choosing. Then share how that letter gives us insight into the life of early Christians in the Roman Empire. 

World History: Grades 10-12
· Blood and Iron: What were the events leading up to the establishment of the German Empire?

· Blood and Iron: Summarize Bismarck’s Reich (1871-1888).
